question: What Is the WordPress REST API, and Why Does My Site Need It?
metaDescription: It's the standard interface letting other applications read and write WordPress data — the block editor itself depends on it to function at all.
shortAnswer: The REST API is a built-in interface exposing WordPress content and data (posts, pages, users, and more) as structured data other applications can read and write over standard HTTP requests, rather than requiring direct database or PHP-level access. It's not an optional add-on feature at this point — the block editor itself is built on top of the REST API to save and load content, which is why disabling it entirely tends to break core editing functionality, not just external integrations.

bodyHtml:
How the REST API Fits Into WordPress

Before the REST API, interacting with WordPress data programmatically generally meant working directly with PHP functions on the server itself. The REST API exposes that same data through standard HTTP endpoints returning JSON, which any application — a mobile app, a separate front-end framework, a third-party integration, or the block editor's own JavaScript interface — can read and write without needing direct server-side access.

Why This Matters for a Typical Site

  • The block editor depends on it entirely — every save, every content load in the editing interface happens through REST API calls behind the scenes, which is why blanket-disabling the REST API breaks core editing, not just optional integrations.
  • Many plugins use it for their own functionality, including some checkout and dynamic-content features that rely on REST endpoints for AJAX-style interactions.
  • It enables headless WordPress setups, where WordPress serves purely as a content backend for a completely separate front-end application, a growing architectural pattern for some projects.
  • Security concerns sometimes lead people to disable it entirely, which is generally the wrong response — properly securing specific endpoints or restricting access where genuinely needed is a better approach than disabling a feature core functionality now depends on.

Working With the REST API Safely

  1. Don't disable the REST API entirely as a security measure, since this risks breaking the block editor and other legitimate functionality.
  2. Restrict specific endpoints or data exposure if there's a genuine concern about sensitive data being accessible, rather than a blanket disable.
  3. Keep WordPress core and plugins updated, since REST API security issues (like any other) are addressed through normal update cycles.

Need REST API access configured or secured properly for a specific integration? See WordPress bug fix.
